standard.title: Carbon Cycle
standard.description: represent the carbon cycle and examine how key processes including combustion, photosynthesis and respiration rely on interactions between Earth's spheres (the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere)
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe the water cycle and rock cycle processes (AC9S4U02, AC9S8U04). They have not yet examined Earth as a system of interacting spheres or traced an element through biogeochemical cycling.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students represent the carbon cycle, identify Earth's four spheres and the interactions between them, explain how photosynthesis, respiration and combustion move carbon between spheres, and examine the impact of human activity on the carbon cycle — including greenhouse gas production and carbon sequestration strategies.

nodes.label: Earth operates as a system of interacting spheres
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe Earth's four spheres (geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere) and give examples of interactions between them.
nodes.minimum_width: Students name and describe Earth's four spheres and give at least one example of an interaction between two different spheres.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the four spheres and give multiple examples of interactions — volcanic eruption releasing CO₂ (geosphere → atmosphere), evaporation (hydrosphere → atmosphere), plants taking up water from soil (biosphere ↔ geosphere/hydrosphere) — and explain the carbon cycle as an example of multi-sphere interaction.
wider: Conduct a field investigation to evaluate carbon sequestration in a local ecosystem — measuring tree biomass, leaf litter and soil depth to estimate carbon storage
Examine how First Nations Australians' firestick farming uses fire-mediated chemical reactions to facilitate energy and nutrient transfer between spheres
Investigate how climate models represent interactions between Earth's spheres — connecting the sphere framework to climate prediction (AC9S10U04)
nodes.hinge_reason: The four-sphere framework is the organisational model that Node 2 uses to trace carbon movements. Students who cannot identify which sphere stores carbon in a given form cannot follow how photosynthesis, respiration and combustion transfer carbon between named spheres — the cycle representation in Node 2 collapses without this scaffolding.

response_modes.reason: Students name the four spheres as a list without understanding them as interacting systems. Making the interaction logic explicit — a process moves something from one sphere to another, and that movement can be traced — is the scaffold for representing the carbon cycle as a dynamic system rather than a static diagram.

success_criteria: Names Earth's four spheres and briefly describes each
Gives at least two examples of interactions between different spheres

nodes.label: Photosynthesis, respiration and combustion move carbon between spheres
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the role of photosynthesis, respiration and combustion in moving carbon between spheres, and represent these processes in the carbon cycle.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain how each of the three key processes (photosynthesis, respiration, combustion) moves carbon between named spheres, and represent this in a carbon cycle diagram.
nodes.typical_width: Students represent the complete carbon cycle showing carbon stores and flows; explain how photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere into the biosphere; how respiration returns it; how combustion (natural and human-caused) releases stored carbon; and how carbon is stored in the geosphere (fossil fuels, limestone) over geological time.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' traditional fire regimes affect carbon cycling differently from European-style bushfire management — examining the greenhouse gas emission implications
Calculate an individual carbon footprint and examine which human activities contribute most to atmospheric CO₂ — connecting abstract cycle to personal action
Examine carbon capture and storage technologies as human interventions in the carbon cycle — evaluating their effectiveness and limitations
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to explain how human combustion has altered the natural carbon cycle. Students who cannot accurately represent the natural cycle — including where carbon is stored and how it moves — cannot identify what human activity has changed or explain why increased atmospheric CO₂ amplifies the greenhouse effect.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly know photosynthesis and respiration as opposite processes without seeing them as part of a cycle that moves carbon between spheres. The reasoning chain — carbon is in different forms in different spheres → processes transfer it between spheres → the total amount is conserved but the distribution changes — is the scaffold that makes the carbon cycle genuinely explanatory.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The traditional fire regime comparison provides a sophisticated First Nations direction with direct relevance to contemporary climate science. Carbon footprint calculation connects the abstract cycle to personal agency and is directly elaboration-grounded.
success_criteria: Explains how photosynthesis, respiration and combustion each move carbon between named spheres
Represents the carbon cycle in a diagram showing at least four processes and three carbon stores

nodes.label: Human activity has altered the carbon cycle and greenhouse effect
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how human activity has altered the natural carbon cycle — increasing atmospheric CO₂ through combustion and land clearing — describe the greenhouse effect, and identify carbon sequestration as a response strategy.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain how human combustion of fossil fuels increases atmospheric CO₂, describe the greenhouse effect, and name one carbon sequestration strategy.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain how burning fossil fuels and land clearing shift the balance of the carbon cycle; describe how increased atmospheric CO₂ amplifies the greenhouse effect; examine the scientific consensus on global warming; identify natural and technological carbon sequestration approaches; and connect to the policy/adoption analysis in AC9S9H03.
wider: Investigate how technological advances in monitoring greenhouse gas emissions have contributed to the reinstatement of traditional fire management practices (AC9S9H02)
Analyse atmospheric CO₂ data from ice cores and monitoring stations to identify patterns and trends (AC9S9I05)
Examine how government initiatives like Landcare support adoption of land restoration practices that improve carbon sequestration (AC9S9H03)
success_criteria: Explains how human combustion of fossil fuels alters the natural carbon cycle
Describes the greenhouse effect and explains why increased CO₂ amplifies it
Names at least one carbon sequestration strategy and explains how it works
